competitors.name: LoanBack
competitors.what_they_do: DIY promissory note and loan agreement builder for friends and family loans. LoanBuilder ($29.95 one-time) auto-calculates interest, payments and amortization, and adds online collaboration, payment reminders and alerts, and a transaction history. Blank Word forms cost $14.95. Payments are logged manually. Its how-it-works page (https://www.loanback.com/how-it-works) says it does not collect payments. I found no AFR or imputed-interest engine, gift-vs-loan flow, forgiveness letters, Form 709 or Medicaid flags, or sibling ledger. Its media page (https://www.loanback.com/media-center) cites Newsweek, CNN Money, Barron's, SmartMoney and Bankrate.
competitors.scale_or_funding: Site claims $1.8B to $2.1B in loans formalized and more than 10 years in market (two pages give different figures). Founded by the team behind Yahoo! Finance. Funding not verified.

competitors.name: FamZoo
competitors.what_they_do: Family prepaid card and finance app aimed at kids and teens. It lists 'Family Loan Tracking' and 'Parent Paid Interest'. I found no mention of adult children, AFR compliance, promissory notes, tax or Medicaid flags, or sibling equalization.
competitors.scale_or_funding: $5.99/mo per family ($4.99/mo on annual prepay). Funding not verified.

competitors.name: Wealth.com
competitors.what_they_do: AI estate and tax planning platform for wills, trusts and powers of attorney, with scenario modeling. It is advisor-led only: clients can access it only through an advisor or attorney. The homepage does not mention intrafamily loans, gift tracking or promissory notes, but it could add them as a feature.
competitors.scale_or_funding: Says it serves firms with more than $15T in combined AUM. Funding not verified.

competitors.name: Vanilla
competitors.what_they_do: Estate planning software for advisors and RIAs, with an estate health check, document builder, AI plan review and GRAT/SLAT modeling. The homepage does not mention intrafamily loans or gift ledgers. It sells to advisors, not consumers.
competitors.scale_or_funding: Pricing not displayed. Funding not verified.

competitors.name: LoanWell (institutional, not family)
competitors.what_they_do: Loan origination and servicing software for CDFIs, credit unions and community banks, including ACH payments and e-sign closing. It is not a family-loan product, but it shows the servicing rails exist as B2B software that a credit-union channel could use.

white_space: Research was limited: the WebSearch budget was exhausted (200 of 200) before any planned search ran, so I worked only from direct fetches of specific pages. I did not search Crunchbase, YC, Product Hunt, forums or RFPs, and I could not check LegalZoom, Rocket Lawyer or Nolo because those URLs returned 404 or 403. What the evidence shows: (1) The document layer is already commoditized. LoanBack sells a note plus amortization schedule for $15 to $30 and has 10+ years of traction, so the free AFR calculator and $49 note pack in the 30-day plan would compete head-on with it. (2) Nothing I found does the parts that are the real product. I checked LoanBack, FamZoo, Wealth.com and Vanilla, and none advertises these: real ACH autopay between parent and adult child; annual interest statements for both parties; a December forgiveness engine that applies the annual gift exclusion; a gift-vs-loan classification flow tied to Form 709 and Medicaid look-back flags; a mortgage gift-letter generator; a sibling advancement ledger that estates can equalize from; a one-click export to the family's estate attorney. (3) The sibling ledger and the classification audit trail appear genuinely unserved for ordinary families. The advisor-only estate tools (Wealth.com, Vanilla) do not sell to a 62-year-old parent or her adult child. (4) Coverage gap: I could not confirm the absence of niche competitors. Private-note servicers, small startups and attorney-firm tools may exist that my fetches missed.
evidence_of_demand: Moderate, and mostly indirect. (1) LoanBack's site claims $1.8B to $2.1B in loans formalized over 10+ years, and press (Newsweek, CNN Money, Barron's, SmartMoney, Bankrate) recommends it for family loans. It charges $14.95 to $29.95 one-time, so people do pay to paper family loans, but at a low price point. Sources: https://www.loanback.com and https://www.loanback.com/media-center. (2) NAR's Profile of Home Buyers and Sellers (July 2024 to June 2025) reports a record median first-time buyer age of 40 and a first-time buyer share of 21%, and notes gifts or loans from relatives or friends as an important source of down payment help. I could not confirm the idea's 22% figure. Source: https://www.nar.realtor/research-and-statistics/research-reports/highlights-from-the-profile-of-home-buyers-and-sellers. (3) Wikipedia cites a Federal Reserve study that around 30% of first-time buyers received direct parental help with a down payment (2009 to 2016), and puts UK family help at about 52% of first-time buyers. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bank_of_Mum_and_Dad. (4) The IRS publishes AFRs monthly, and October 2026 is the latest posted, which supports the below-market-loan compliance point. Source: https://www.irs.gov/applicable-federal-rates. (5) FamZoo charges $5.99/mo per family and lists family loan tracking, which suggests some willingness to pay a monthly fee for family money tools. Source: https://famzoo.com. Not found: any direct evidence (forum complaints, RFPs) that families will pay $20/mo for servicing. The Medicaid look-back and Form 709 claims are legally plausible, but I could not verify them from sources in this session because the Elder Law Answers page returned no usable content.
sharper_angle: Do not lead with the loan. Lead with the sibling advancement ledger and a gift-vs-loan classification record, sold as an estate-ready evidence file. (1) Drop the free AFR calculator and $49 note pack as the acquisition wedge, since LoanBack already owns that search intent at $15 to $30. (2) Offer a free or cheap ledger of every gift, loan, forgiveness and gift letter, with a timestamped classification audit trail. Its purpose is to prove, at the estate or Medicaid look-back stage, what was a loan and what was a gift. No competitor I found offers this. (3) Make the elder-law and estate attorney the primary channel (B2B2C), with per-client-seat pricing and a record the client can export straight into the attorney's file. The advisor-only platforms (Wealth.com, Vanilla) do not reach mass-affluent families. (4) Avoid money movement at launch: detect payments through bank-link transaction matching instead of collecting ACH. That sidesteps loan-servicing licensing, money-transmission and unauthorized-practice-of-law exposure until there is a licensed servicer or credit-union partner, and real autopay can be added later through that partner. (5) Price the paid moment on year-end and estate events (forgiveness letters, interest statements, attorney export) rather than a flat $20/mo, because LoanBack shows one-time pricing is the norm in this category. Before building, rerun the search pass once the search budget is restored (Crunchbase, Product Hunt, r/personalfinance, elder-law attorney forums), and specifically look for private-note servicers and attorney-firm tools that might already bundle an advancement ledger.
